title: CSS: Selectors, the Cascade, the Box Model and Layout
sub: Attach styles, target exactly the elements you mean, predict which rule wins, size boxes, and lay out a responsive dashboard with a dark theme
goals: Attach CSS to a page and read any rule as selector, declarations, properties and values
Target elements with class, attribute, combinator and pseudo-class selectors, including :is(), :where() and :has()
Predict the winning declaration from origin, specificity, order and inheritance, and fix a losing rule without !important
Size boxes with the box model and lay them out with flexbox, grid and positioning
Make a dashboard responsive with media queries and clamp(), and theme it with custom properties
Find out why an element looks the way it does with the Elements pane and getComputedStyle()

blocks.text: In this chapter you will style the home-lab pages from [HTML](#html): a device table, status badges driven by `data-state` attributes, a navigation bar, a card grid and a responsive dashboard with a dark theme. CSS reads like a list of settings, but the browser runs it as an engine with three stages. **Matching** finds every rule whose selector fits an element. The **cascade** picks one winning value per property per element. **Layout** turns those values into boxes with positions and sizes. When a page looks wrong, one of those three stages did something you did not predict, and every technique in this chapter is about predicting them.

Every playground below has a DevTools drawer. Click an element in **Elements** to see its box model and computed values, then type `getComputedStyle($0).color` in **Console**. Change a value in the CSS tab and watch the preview update. Predict first, then look.
How CSS reaches the page
A page can get CSS in three ways, and you will meet all three in real code:

blocks.code: offline

blocks.text: When the HTML parser meets `<link rel="stylesheet">` it downloads the file in parallel and keeps parsing, but the browser **will not paint** until the stylesheet is parsed. CSS is *render-blocking* on purpose, so unstyled content never flashes. The CSS parser turns the text into the **CSSOM** (CSS Object Model), a tree of rule objects that JavaScript can read through `document.styleSheets`. The page load step-through in [How the Web Works](#web-intro) shows where this happens.

Prefer external files. One `lab.css` serves every page, the browser caches it (a repeat visit costs a `304 Not Modified` or nothing), you edit one place, and a Content-Security-Policy can forbid inline styles entirely. `<style>` suits a single page or a demo. Inline `style=""` attributes beat every selector, which makes them hard to override; leave them to JavaScript. `@import url(other.css);` inside CSS waits for the first file before fetching the second; prefer several `<link>` tags.
Anatomy of a rule

tokens.exp: selector: which elements the rule applies to (here: cells inside rows with class offline inside .devices)
a property name, then a colon
its value, ended by a semicolon

blocks.text: A **rule** (also called a ruleset) is a selector plus a declaration block. Each **declaration** is a `property: value` pair. Lines that start with `@` are **at-rules**: `@media`, `@import`, `@keyframes`, `@font-face`, `@supports`, `@layer`. Comments are `/* ... */`; there is no `//` comment in CSS, and a stray `//` silently breaks the rule after it.

CSS never stops at an error. The parser **drops what it does not understand and carries on**: an unknown property or invalid value loses just that declaration, and one invalid selector in a comma-separated list throws away the whole rule. That forgiveness keeps old browsers working with new CSS, and it is also why a typo never produces an error message. You can watch the parser throw things away:

blocks.page: • nas 192.168.1.60

blocks.text: The misspelled `colr` vanished from the first rule, the second rule disappeared entirely because `:not-a-real-thing` is not a valid selector, and the last rule survived without its final semicolon. The `li` is not red: its colour, `rgb(29, 42, 49)`, is the dark grey this book's practice frame gives its `body`, inherited because nothing valid set `color` on the `li`.

blocks.name: <link rel="stylesheet">
blocks.sum: Load an external stylesheet into the page; the normal way to attach CSS.

how.text: The element goes in `<head>`. The browser fetches `href` like any other resource (it appears in the Network pane with type `stylesheet`), parses it into the CSSOM and holds back the first paint until it is ready. Several links are applied in document order, so a later file wins ties against an earlier one.

The `media` attribute still downloads the file but applies it only when the media query matches, which keeps print styles out of the screen render path. Relative `href` values resolve against the page URL, so `css/lab.css` on `http://localhost:8000/admin/` means `/admin/css/lab.css`.

blocks.text: Selectors: choosing the elements
A selector is a pattern tested against each element. The basic pieces:

head: Selector
Matches
Example
rows: elements that have the attribute, any value

blocks.text: Write several simple selectors together with no space (a **compound selector**) and an element must satisfy all of them: `tr.offline[data-id]` means a `tr` with class `offline` and a `data-id` attribute.
Combinators: relationships in the tree

head: Combinator
Name
Matches
rows: a `B` immediately after an `A`, same parent
anything matching `A` or `B` (not a combinator, a list)

nav a → ⟪g:Home⟫, ⟪g:Devices⟫, ⟪g:Logs⟫ (every a inside nav) ├── Home nav > a → ⟪g:Home⟫ only (the others have ul/li parents) ├──

blocks.text: Browsers match **right to left**: for `nav ul a` they test each `a` first, then walk up its ancestors looking for a `ul` and a `nav`. Most elements fail the first test, so this is cheap. A parent selector (`:has()`) asks the opposite question, which is why it arrived decades later.
Pseudo-classes: state and position
A **pseudo-class** (one colon) selects elements by something that is not a plain attribute: user interaction, position among siblings, form state, or a logical test.

head: Group
Pseudo-classes
Notes
rows: `:focus-visible` shows a focus ring for keyboard users without flashing one on every mouse click
driven by the HTML validation attributes

blocks.text: `:nth-child(An+B)` picks the children whose 1-based position equals `A*n + B` for some `n = 0, 1, 2, ...`. So `2n` (or `even`) is 2, 4, 6; `2n+1` (or `odd`) is 1, 3, 5; `-n+3` is the first three; `3` is just the third. The newer form `:nth-child(2 of .server)` counts only the children that match `.server`. `:nth-of-type()` counts only siblings of the same element type, which is handy when headings and paragraphs are mixed.
The four logical pseudo-classes save a lot of repetition:

items.text: `:not(.server)` matches elements that do *not* match the list.
`:is(header, main, footer) a` is shorthand for `header a, main a, footer a`, and an invalid entry inside `:is()` does not kill the rule (the list is *forgiving*).
`:where(...)` matches exactly like `:is()` but adds **zero specificity**, which makes it perfect for defaults that anything can override.

`:has(...)` matches an element if the relative selector inside matches something around it: `.card:has(.badge[data-state="down"])` is a card that *contains* a down badge, `h2:has(+ table)` is a heading directly followed by a table, and `label:has(input:invalid)` styles a label whose input is invalid. All current browsers support it (Chrome 105, Safari 15.4, Firefox 121).

blocks.text: Pseudo-elements: parts that are not in the HTML
A **pseudo-element** (two colons) styles a piece of an element, or generates a box that does not exist in the markup:

items.text: `::before` and `::after` create a first or last child box, and **only exist if `content` is set** (`content: ""` for a decorative box). Never put essential information there: screen readers announce it inconsistently.
`::placeholder` styles an input's placeholder, `::marker` the bullet or number of a list item, `::selection` highlighted text, `::first-line` and `::first-letter` typography.

blocks.name: [attr] selectors
blocks.sum: Select elements by the presence or value of an attribute, including data-* attributes.

how.text: The browser compares the attribute's current string value: `=` exact, `^=` prefix, `$=` suffix, `*=` substring, `~=` one word in a space-separated list (how `.class` works internally). Add ` i` before the bracket for an ASCII case-insensitive match. Each attribute selector counts as one class in specificity.

Attribute selectors make **state in the markup** visible to CSS: JavaScript sets `el.dataset.state = 'down'`, which writes `data-state="down"`, and the matching rule applies on the next style recalculation without any class juggling.

how.code:
.badge[data-state="down"] { background: #fde7ea; color: #b00020; }
a[href^="http"]:not([href*="lab.local"])::after { content: " ↗"; }

examples.desc: Count the devices marked down
Collect the names of every device that is not up

gotchas: Values with spaces or special characters need quotes, and the comparison is case-sensitive unless you add ` i`. `[data-state=Down]` does not match `data-state="down"`.

blocks.name: :nth-child()
blocks.sum: Select children by their 1-based position among their siblings, optionally counting only siblings that match a selector.

how.text: For each element the browser takes its position among all element siblings (text nodes do not count), starting at 1, and checks whether some `n >= 0` makes `A*n + B` equal that position. `odd` is `2n+1`, `even` is `2n`, `-n+3` is "the first three", `n+4` is "the fourth onwards". `:nth-last-child()` counts from the end.
With `of S` the browser first filters the siblings by `S` and counts only those, which fixes zebra striping on a table where some rows are hidden: `tr:nth-child(odd of :not([hidden]))`.

how.code:
tbody tr:nth-child(even) { background: #f2f6f8; }
.ports li:nth-child(-n+3) { font-weight: 700; }

examples.desc: Check which rows a pattern hits before writing the rule
Read the first cell of every odd row of a table

gotchas: `p:nth-child(2)` means "an element that is the second child *and* is a `p`", not "the second `p`". Use `p:nth-of-type(2)` for the second paragraph.

blocks.name: :is() :where() :not()
blocks.sum: Match an element against a list of selectors: any of them (:is, :where) or none of them (:not).

how.text: `:is()` and `:where()` match when any selector in the list matches. They differ only in specificity: `:is()` counts as its **most specific argument**, `:where()` always counts **zero**. `:not()` matches when none of the list matches and also takes the specificity of its most specific argument.
`:is()` and `:where()` use a forgiving list, so one unsupported selector inside them is ignored instead of invalidating the rule. `:not()` is not forgiving.

how.code:
:where(ul, ol)[class] { margin: 0; padding: 0; list-style: none; }   /* (0,0,0) + attribute = (0,1,0) */
:is(header, footer) a:not(.btn) { color: inherit; }

examples.code: [...document.querySelectorAll(':is(h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6)')].map((h) => h.tagName).join(' > ');

gotchas: `:is(#main, .card) p` has specificity (1,0,1) even when it matched through `.card`, because `:is()` always takes its most specific argument. Use `:where()` when you want a rule that is easy to override.

blocks.name: :has()
blocks.sum: Select an element by what it contains or what follows it: the long-awaited parent selector.

how.text: The argument is a *relative* selector, anchored at the element being tested: `.card:has(.badge)` asks "does this card have a `.badge` descendant?", `:has(> img)` a direct child, `:has(+ p)` a next sibling, `:has(~ .error)` any later sibling. Specificity is that of the most specific argument, like `:is()`.

Browsers keep extra bookkeeping so that changing a descendant (say, a checkbox being ticked) re-evaluates the ancestor's style, which is what makes this usable for interactive styling with no JavaScript.

examples.desc: Find the table rows that contain an offline cell
Print the device name from each card that contains a down badge

gotchas: `:has()` cannot be nested inside another `:has()`, and pseudo-elements are not allowed in it.

blocks.name: ::before ::after
blocks.sum: Generate a first or last child box inside an element, styled entirely from CSS.

how.text: The browser creates the box only when `content` is not `none`. The box is inline by default, sits inside the element (so it inherits its font and colour), and takes part in layout like a real child. It does not exist in the DOM, so JavaScript cannot select it; it can only read its style with `getComputedStyle(el, '::before')`.

Typical uses are decoration that must not live in the markup: status dots, required-field asterisks, external-link arrows, tooltips with `content: attr(data-tip)`, clearing floats. Replaced elements such as `` and `` cannot have them.

how.code:
.badge::before { content: "●"; margin-right: 6px; color: currentColor; }
label.required::after { content: " *"; color: #b00020; }

examples.desc: Read what a pseudo-element displays
List the generated content of every badge on the page

gotchas: Generated text is invisible to copy and paste and inconsistently read by screen readers. Status that matters ("offline") belongs in the HTML; the dot can be CSS.

The cascade: which declaration wins

Many rules can set the same property on the same element. For every element and every property, the browser collects all matching declarations and sorts them. The first step that separates them decides:

blocks.code:
every declaration of `color` that matches <button id="save" class="btn primary">
        │
        ▼
 ⟪c:1. origin and importance⟫  browser defaults  <  user styles  <  ⟪g:your CSS (author)⟫
                            then !important reverses it: author !important < user !important < browser !important
 ⟪c:2. inline style=""⟫        a style attribute beats every selector (same importance)
 ⟪c:3. cascade layers⟫         @layer order; styles outside any layer beat layered ones
 ⟪c:4. specificity⟫            (IDs, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, types/pseudo-elements)
 ⟪c:5. order of appearance⟫    the later declaration wins
        │
        ▼
 ⟪y:cascaded value⟫ ── none at all? ──▶ inherit from the parent (inherited properties) or use the initial value
        │
        ▼
 ⟪y:computed value⟫ (em → px, keywords resolved)  ──▶  ⟪y:used value⟫ (after layout: % widths → px)

blocks.text: Usually steps 1 to 3 tie (all your CSS, no inline styles, no layers), so specificity decides, and when specificity ties, **the last one wins**, including across files: the second `<link>` beats the first.
Specificity
**Specificity** is a triple `(a, b, c)` computed from the selector:

items.text: **a**: the number of ID selectors (`#save`).
**b**: classes (`.btn`), attribute selectors (`[type="submit"]`) and pseudo-classes (`:hover`).
**c**: type selectors (`button`) and pseudo-elements (`::before`).

blocks.text: The universal selector `*` and combinators (` `, `>`, `+`, `~`) add nothing. `:where()` adds nothing; `:is()`, `:not()` and `:has()` add their most specific argument. Triples compare **column by column, like version numbers**: `(1,0,0)` beats `(0,15,0)`, because a column is only consulted when every column to its left is equal. It is not a decimal number.

Type `#toolbar button` into A and `.btn.btn-primary` into B: A wins with (1,0,1) against (0,2,0), and that is the most common real-world specificity fight. You will win it properly in the Practice section.
The cascade in action, read through `getComputedStyle()`:

blocks.page:
<style id="lab">
  button        { color: rgb(0, 0, 0); }
  .btn.primary  { color: rgb(176, 0, 32); }
  #save         { color: rgb(0, 128, 0); }
  .btn          { color: rgb(0, 90, 160); }
</style>
<button id="save" class="btn primary">Save</button>
blocks.out:
stylesheet only: rgb(0, 128, 0)
plus inline style: rgb(128, 0, 128)
plus !important: rgb(255, 140, 0)

blocks.text: `#save` (1,0,0) beats `.btn.primary` (0,2,0) even though it comes earlier, and `.btn` loses to both despite coming last. The inline style beats every selector. The `!important` declaration was inserted at position 0 of the sheet, the earliest possible place, and it still wins over the inline style, because importance is decided before inline styles and order.

`!important` jumps a declaration to a higher layer of the cascade, and the only way to beat it is another `!important` with higher specificity or a later position. Two of those and you have an arms race nobody can follow. Legitimate uses are narrow: overriding inline styles injected by a third-party widget, utility classes that must always apply, and the reduced-motion reset at the end of this chapter. When a rule loses, raise its specificity a little or reorder; first find out *why* it loses.

`@layer reset, base, components;` declares cascade layers: any rule in `components` beats any rule in `base` whatever their specificities, and unlayered rules beat all layers. Large codebases use it to end specificity wars.
Inheritance and the global keywords

When no declaration sets a property on an element at all, two things can happen. **Inherited** properties take the parent's computed value: `color`, all `font-*` properties, `line-height`, `letter-spacing`, `text-align`, `visibility`, `cursor`, `list-style` and every custom property (`--name`). **Non-inherited** properties take their *initial value* from the specification: `margin` and `padding` (0), `border` (none), `background` (transparent), `width` (auto), `display` (inline), `position` (static). That split is why setting `color` on `body` colours the whole page while setting `border` on `body` borders only the body.
Four keywords work on every property:

head: Keyword
Means
rows: take the parent's computed value, even for a non-inherited property
the specification's initial value (not the browser's default for that element)
`inherit` for inherited properties, `initial` for the rest
roll back to what the browser's own stylesheet would give this element

blocks.text: The difference between `initial` and `revert` surprises everyone once:

blocks.page:
plain div
initial
revert
unset
blocks.out:
plain block
initial inline
revert block
unset inline
13.3333px

blocks.text: The initial value of `display` in the specification is `inline`; `block` for a `div` comes from the browser's stylesheet, which `revert` restores. The last line shows another inheritance trap: the body says 18 px, yet the button's font is 13.3333 px, because the browser stylesheet gives form controls their own font size. That is why every reset contains `button, input, select, textarea { font: inherit; }`.

blocks.name: inherit initial unset revert
blocks.sum: Keywords valid for every property that pull a value from the parent, the specification or the browser's defaults.
blocks.syntax: property: inherit | initial | unset | revert | revert-layer      all: unset | revert

how.text: These keywords take part in the cascade like any value and are resolved at computed-value time. `inherit` forces inheritance, `initial` uses the property's spec-defined starting value, `unset` acts as `inherit` or `initial` depending on whether the property inherits, `revert` restores the user-agent stylesheet's value, and `revert-layer` rolls back to the previous cascade layer.
The shorthand `all` applies one keyword to every property at once (except `direction`, `unicode-bidi` and custom properties): `all: revert` on an element undoes the author styles that reached it.

how.code:
button, input, select, textarea { font: inherit; color: inherit; }
.plain-link { all: unset; cursor: pointer; }

examples.desc: See what the browser computed for a keyword
Find form controls whose font size differs from the body's

gotchas: `display: initial` gives `inline`, not `block`. Use `revert` to get "the normal display for this element".

head: Unit
Relative to
Use it for
rows: the CSS pixel, 1/96 inch; a Retina display paints each with 2×2 or 3×3 device pixels

blocks.text: `em` compounds: an element at `0.75em` inside another at `0.75em` ends up at 0.5625 of the outer size. `rem` never compounds, which is why it is the safer default for font sizes. Both are computed to pixels before inheritance, which you can watch:

blocks.page:
panel label deep
calc
clamp
min
blocks.out:
.panel  font 20px padding 20px
.label  font 15px padding 15px
.deep   font 11.25px
.calc  width 232px
.clamp width 200px  .min width 150px

blocks.text: `1.25rem` is 20 px, so the panel's `1em` padding is 20 px. The label is `0.75em` of 20 px, 15 px, and its own `1em` padding follows its own font size. The math functions mix units freely: `calc()` does arithmetic, `min()` and `max()` pick the smaller or larger, and `clamp(MIN, PREFERRED, MAX)` keeps a preferred value between two limits. Here 50% of the 400 px container is 200 px, inside the 100 to 300 px range.

blocks.name: clamp()
blocks.sum: Keep a value at a preferred size, but never below a minimum or above a maximum.
blocks.syntax: clamp(MIN, PREFERRED, MAX)        same as  max(MIN, min(PREFERRED, MAX))

how.text: The browser computes all three values (they may mix units and contain `calc()` arithmetic without writing `calc`), then returns the preferred one limited to the range. With a viewport unit in the middle, the value grows with the window between the two limits, which gives fluid typography without a single media query.
Mixing a `rem` part into the preferred value keeps it responsive to the user's font-size setting; a pure `vw` font size ignores browser zoom on some browsers, which is an accessibility failure.

how.code:
h1      { font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 1rem + 2.5vw, 2.5rem); }
.layout { width: clamp(320px, 92%, 72rem); margin-inline: auto; }

gotchas: If MIN is larger than MAX, MIN wins. Check the order when a value refuses to shrink.

blocks.text: Whatever you write, `getComputedStyle()` reports sRGB colours as `rgb(r, g, b)` (or `rgba()` with alpha), which is the format to compare against in scripts and checks.
The box model
Layout turns every element into a rectangular **box** with four layers:

By default (`box-sizing: content-box`) `width` and `height` size only the content; padding and border are added outside. A 200 px wide card with 20 px padding is 248 px on screen, and three "33.33%" columns with padding overflow their row. `box-sizing: border-box` makes `width` mean the border box, so padding eats into the content instead. Nearly every modern stylesheet starts with `*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }`.

blocks.text: `offsetWidth` is the border box, `clientWidth` the padding box (content plus padding). The last line shows **margin collapsing**: in normal block flow, the bottom margin of one box and the top margin of the next merge into the larger of the two (30 px, not 50 px). The same happens between a parent and its first or last child when no padding or border separates them, which is the classic "my child's margin leaks out of the parent" bug. Margins never collapse horizontally, and never inside flex or grid containers, which is why the flex column shows 50 px.
Other parts of the box you need:

items.text: `margin: auto` on the left and right of a block with a width centres it: `width: min(100%, 60rem); margin-inline: auto;`.
`overflow: visible | hidden | auto | scroll | clip` decides what happens to content larger than the box. `auto` adds scrollbars only when needed.
`outline` draws outside the border without taking space, which is why focus rings use it. Never remove it without a replacement: `:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid #0a7f9c; outline-offset: 2px; }`.
Logical properties follow writing direction: `margin-inline` (left and right in English), `padding-block`, `inline-size`.

blocks.name: box-sizing
blocks.sum: Choose whether width and height size the content box or the whole border box.

how.text: With `content-box` (the initial value) the used border-box width is `width + padding-left + padding-right + border-left + border-right`. With `border-box` the browser subtracts padding and border from `width` to get the content width (never below zero), so the element occupies exactly the width you wrote.
It is not inherited, which is why the standard reset targets every element and both pseudo-elements explicitly.

how.code: *, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }

blocks.name: margin padding
blocks.sum: Space outside the border (margin) and inside it (padding), with one- to four-value shorthands.
blocks.syntax: margin: ALL | VERT HORIZ | TOP HORIZ BOTTOM | TOP RIGHT BOTTOM LEFT      (same for padding)

how.text: The four-value order runs **clockwise from the top**: top, right, bottom, left. Missing values copy their opposite: two values are vertical then horizontal, three are top, horizontal, bottom. Percentages resolve against the containing block's *width*, even for top and bottom.

Padding is inside the element, takes its background and can never be negative. Margin is outside, always transparent, can be negative (pulling neighbours closer or overlapping), can be `auto` to absorb free space, and collapses vertically in block flow.

how.code:
.card   { padding: 8px 12px; margin: 0 0 16px; }   /* 8 top/bottom, 12 left/right; 16 below */
.center { margin-inline: auto; width: min(100%, 40rem); }

blocks.text: Display and normal flow
Every box has an **outer display type**, how it behaves among its siblings, and an **inner display type**, how it lays out its children. Without any CSS, boxes follow **normal flow**:

items.text: **Block** boxes (`div`, `p`, `h1`, `ul`, `table`, `section`) stack vertically, each starting on a new line and taking the full available width. `width`, `height`, margins and padding all apply.
**Inline** boxes (`span`, `a`, `strong`, `code`) flow inside lines of text and wrap. `width` and `height` are ignored, and vertical padding and margins do not push surrounding lines apart.
**Inline-block** flows inline like a word but respects width, height and vertical spacing, which is useful for badges and buttons.

blocks.text: `display: flex` and `display: grid` make the box a block on the outside and a flex or grid **container** on the inside. `display: none` removes the box completely: no space, no events, not in the accessibility tree. Compare `visibility: hidden` (invisible but still takes space) and `opacity: 0` (invisible, takes space and still receives clicks).

blocks.text: The span's computed `width` still says `200px`, yet its box is only as wide as its text: the property does not apply to inline boxes, which is exactly what Chrome's Styles pane flags with an "inactive" hint. Computed values tell you what the cascade decided; `offsetWidth` and `getBoundingClientRect()` tell you what layout did. The hidden element has no box at all, so its measured width is 0.

blocks.name: display
blocks.sum: Set how an element's box takes part in layout (block, inline, flex, grid, none, ...).
blocks.syntax: display: block | inline | inline-block | flex | inline-flex | grid | inline-grid | none | contents | flow-root

how.text: The value sets the outer type (block or inline participation in its parent) and the inner type (how children are laid out: normal flow, flex or grid). The two-value form says it explicitly: `display: inline flex` is the same as `inline-flex`.

`none` removes the element and its whole subtree from rendering. `contents` removes only the element's own box, so its children behave as children of the grandparent (handy for grid layouts, but it can remove semantics from the accessibility tree for some elements). `flow-root` makes a block that contains its floats and stops margin collapsing through it.

examples.desc: Ask what display an element ended up with

gotchas: The `hidden` attribute is implemented as `display: none` in the browser stylesheet, so any author rule like `.panel { display: flex }` overrides it and the "hidden" panel shows. The `[hidden] { display: none !important; }` line in many resets exists for this.

blocks.text: Flexbox: one-dimensional layout

`display: flex` turns an element into a **flex container** and its direct children into **flex items**. Items are laid out along a **main axis** (a row by default), and aligned on the perpendicular **cross axis**.
Container properties:

head: Property
Values
Effect
rows: which way the main axis runs
allow items to move to new lines instead of shrinking
free space on the main axis
position on the cross axis (default `stretch`: equal heights)
space between items (row gap, then column gap)

blocks.text: Item properties: `flex-grow` (share of positive free space), `flex-shrink` (share of overflow to absorb, weighted by size), `flex-basis` (starting size before growing or shrinking), `align-self` (override `align-items` for one item) and `order` (visual order only; keyboard and screen-reader order still follow the HTML, so avoid it for meaningful content).

The algorithm, in short: each item starts at its `flex-basis` (or its content size when the basis is `auto`). The browser subtracts the bases and the gaps from the container's width. Positive free space is handed out in proportion to `flex-grow`; negative free space is taken back in proportion to `flex-shrink × basis`. You can check the arithmetic: a 600 px container, three items with a 100 px basis and 10 px gaps leaves `600 − 300 − 20 = 280` px; with grow factors 1, 2 and 1 the items get 70, 140 and 70 px extra.

blocks.code:
const widths = [...document.querySelectorAll('.row > div')].map((el) => el.getBoundingClientRect().width);
console.log(widths);

blocks.text: Two tricks you will use weekly. An auto margin absorbs all free space on its side, so `margin-left: auto` pushes an item to the far end of a row (the logout button). And flex items refuse to shrink below their content's minimum size, so a long URL overflows the row; give the item `min-width: 0`, then truncate with `overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; white-space: nowrap`.

blocks.name: display: flex
blocks.sum: Lay out an element's direct children in a row or column, distributing space and aligning them.
blocks.syntax: display: flex; flex-direction: row | column; flex-wrap: nowrap | wrap; justify-content: ...; align-items: ...; gap: ...

how.text: The container establishes a flex formatting context: floats and margin collapsing stop applying to its children, and each in-flow child becomes a flex item, including anonymous items for loose text. The browser resolves each item's basis, then distributes positive or negative free space using the items' grow and shrink factors, then aligns items on the cross axis.

Use flexbox when the content decides the size (toolbars, nav bars, a row of badges, a form row with a label, an input and a button). Use grid when you want the layout to decide the size (page skeletons, card grids, dashboards).

.toolbar .spacer { margin-left: auto; }

blocks.name: flex
blocks.sum: Set an item's grow factor, shrink factor and basis in one declaration.
blocks.syntax: flex: none | auto | GROW | GROW SHRINK BASIS      e.g. flex: 1   flex: 0 0 200px

how.text: `flex: 1` expands to `1 1 0%`: start from zero and share all the space by the grow factors, which gives equal columns whatever their content. `flex: auto` is `1 1 auto`: start from the content size and share only the leftover. `flex: none` is `0 0 auto`: keep the content size, never grow or shrink. The initial value is `0 1 auto`.
Grow factors are ratios of the free space, not of the final width, so `flex-grow: 2` makes an item get twice the *extra*, not end up twice as wide, unless the bases are zero.

.main    { flex: 1; min-width: 0; }

blocks.text: Grid: two-dimensional layout

`display: grid` divides the container into **tracks**: columns and rows separated by numbered **lines**. Items are placed into cells automatically, row by row, or explicitly by line numbers or named areas.

head: Property
Example
Meaning
rows: three columns: fixed, then the free space split 1:2
at least 220 px, at most an equal share
as many columns as fit: a responsive grid with no media query
name cells with strings; `.` marks an empty cell
put an item into a named area
place by line numbers or span tracks
size of rows the browser creates as items flow in
gutters between tracks (never at the outer edges)

blocks.text: The `fr` unit shares out the space left after fixed tracks and gaps. The difference between `auto-fit` and `auto-fill` shows only when there are fewer items than columns would fit: `auto-fill` keeps the empty columns, `auto-fit` collapses them to zero so the existing items stretch.

In the first grid, 400 px remain after the fixed column and are split 1:3. In the 704 px containers with 16 px gaps, three 220 px columns fit (`3 × 220 + 2 × 16 = 692`) and four do not. With only two items, `auto-fill` keeps the empty third column (the cards stay 224 px wide), while `auto-fit` collapses it to `0px` and the two cards share the row at 344 px each.

blocks.name: display: grid
blocks.sum: Lay out children on rows and columns of tracks, sized with px, %, fr, minmax() and repeat().
blocks.syntax: display: grid; grid-template-columns: TRACKS; grid-template-rows: TRACKS; gap: ROW COL;

how.text: The container defines explicit tracks; items are auto-placed into the next free cell in row order (`grid-auto-flow: row`), and extra rows are created as needed with the `grid-auto-rows` size. Track sizing resolves fixed sizes first, then content-based (`auto`, `min-content`, `max-content`), then shares the remaining space among `fr` tracks.
`repeat(auto-fit, minmax(MIN, 1fr))` is the single most useful line in CSS layout: as many columns as fit at MIN or wider, stretched to fill the row, wrapping automatically.

blocks.name: grid-template-areas
blocks.sum: Name the cells of a grid with strings, then place items by area name.
blocks.syntax: grid-template-areas: "a a" "b c";   item { grid-area: a; }

how.text: Each string is one row; each whitespace-separated word is one cell; repeating a name across adjacent cells makes that area span them; `.` leaves a cell empty. Every area must be a rectangle and every row must have the same number of cells, or the whole declaration is invalid and dropped.

Because the strings describe the layout visually, a media query can rearrange the whole page by redefining only `grid-template-columns` and `grid-template-areas`, leaving the HTML order (and so the reading order) unchanged.

blocks.text: Positioning and stacking
`position` takes a box out of the normal rules in five ways:

head: Value
Positioned against
In the flow?
rows: its own normal position; the original space stays reserved
the padding box of the nearest **positioned** ancestor (any value except static), else the initial containing block
the viewport (unless an ancestor has `transform`, `filter` or similar, which then contains it)
behaves as relative until scrolling reaches the `top` threshold inside its scroll container, then sticks

blocks.text: The everyday pattern is a `relative` parent with an `absolute` child, which pins a badge or a close button to a corner of a card without affecting layout. `inset: 0` is shorthand for `top: 0; right: 0; bottom: 0; left: 0`, an overlay that fills the parent.

blocks.text: The badge sits 8 px from the card's right edge: `200 − 8 − 20 = 172`. Make the card `static` and the badge's containing block becomes the initial one; `offsetParent` reports `BODY`, and on a real page the badge jumps to the top-right corner of the window.
z-index and stacking contexts

`z-index` orders overlapping positioned boxes (and flex and grid items) along the axis towards you. It only competes **inside the same stacking context**. A new **stacking context** is created by the root element, a positioned element with a `z-index` other than `auto`, `position: fixed` or `sticky`, `opacity` below 1, `transform`, `filter`, `isolation: isolate`, and a few others. Everything inside a context is painted together as one layer of its parent context.

root stacking context

Raising the modal's number does nothing. Move the modal out of that ancestor (to the end of `body`) or remove the property that created the context.

blocks.sum: Take a box out of normal positioning: offset it, pin it to an ancestor or the viewport, or make it stick while scrolling.

how.text: For `relative` the offsets move the painted box but layout still reserves its original space. For `absolute` and `fixed` the box is removed from flow and the offsets are distances from the edges of the **containing block**: the nearest positioned ancestor's padding box (absolute) or the viewport (fixed). `sticky` keeps the box in flow and switches between relative and fixed-like behaviour as its nearest *scrolling* ancestor scrolls past the threshold, and only within its parent's bounds.

blocks.name: z-index
blocks.sum: Order overlapping boxes front to back within their stacking context.

how.text: Applies to positioned boxes and to flex and grid items. Within one stacking context the browser paints, back to front: the context's background, children with negative z-index, block boxes in flow, floats, inline content, then positioned children with `z-index: auto` or 0, then positive z-index in increasing order. Ties paint in document order.
An element with a z-index other than `auto` (when positioned) creates a new stacking context, so its children's z-index values are only compared with each other.

blocks.text: Responsive design

A responsive page adapts to the width of the screen it lands on. Three ingredients do almost all of the work. The viewport `<meta>` tag from [HTML](#html) stops phones from pretending to be 980 px wide. Fluid sizes (`%`, `fr`, `minmax()`, `clamp()`, `max-width: 100%` on images) let most things adapt with no breakpoints at all. **Media queries** handle the rest: a block of rules that applies only when a condition about the device is true.

tokens.exp: a media feature in range syntax; the older form is (min-width: 600px)
the rules that apply while the condition is true

blocks.text: Write **mobile first**: base styles describe the narrow, single-column layout, and `min-width` (or `width >=`) queries add columns as space appears. The base CSS stays simple, and narrow devices download and apply the least. Pick breakpoints where *your content* breaks (the point where a line of cards gets cramped), not at the widths of particular phones.

head: Media feature
Example
Use
rows: layout breakpoints (rem breakpoints follow the user's font size)
System Settings > Accessibility > Display > Reduce motion
touch screens: larger targets, no hover-only menus
hide navigation, show URLs of links

blocks.text: Media queries look at the viewport. A component that must adapt to the space *it* gets (a card in a narrow sidebar or a wide main column) uses a **container query**: give the parent `container-type: inline-size`, then write `@container (width > 400px) { ... }`. All current browsers support them.

To test, make the browser window narrower, or use Chrome's device toolbar (⇧⌘M with DevTools focused) or Safari's Responsive Design Mode (Develop menu, ⌃⌘R). JavaScript can ask the same questions with `matchMedia()`.

blocks.name: @media
blocks.sum: Apply a block of rules only while a condition about the viewport or the user's preferences is true.

how.text: The browser evaluates every media query on load and again whenever the condition can change (window resize, rotation, dark-mode switch, zoom), then re-runs the cascade. Rules inside a query have no extra specificity: they win only by coming later or by being more specific, which is why responsive overrides go *after* the base rules.
Range syntax (`width >= 600px`, `400px <= width < 900px`) is supported by all current browsers and reads better than the `min-width`/`max-width` pairs you will still see in most existing code.

blocks.text: Custom properties and theming
A **custom property** is a property whose name starts with two dashes. You define it like any declaration and read it anywhere with `var()`:

The mechanism explains every behaviour. Custom properties are ordinary properties that **inherit**, so a value set on `:root` reaches every element and a value set on `.alert` overrides it for that subtree. They take part in the cascade, so media queries and selectors can change them. Their value is just a stored token string until a `var()` uses it; the real property is computed **at that moment**, on that element. If the substituted value is invalid for the property, the declaration does not fall back to an earlier rule; it becomes `unset`, a state called *invalid at computed-value time*. And because they live on elements, `var()` cannot be used inside a media query condition.

blocks.name: --* and var()
blocks.sum: Define your own inherited properties and substitute their values into other declarations.

how.text: A custom property's value is an unparsed token string; it inherits like `color` and cascades like any property. `var(--name)` is replaced at computed-value time on each element where it is used, with the fallback used when the property is not defined there. Names are case-sensitive: `--Accent` and `--accent` are different properties.

JavaScript reads them with `getComputedStyle(el).getPropertyValue('--name')` and writes them with `el.style.setProperty('--name', value)`, which makes them the bridge between script state and styling.

blocks.text: Transitions and animation

A **transition** animates a property from its old computed value to its new one whenever it changes, whether because a class was toggled, an attribute changed or `:hover` started to match. An **animation** runs a named sequence of `@keyframes` by itself, optionally forever.

tokens.exp: timing function: ease, linear, ease-in, ease-out, cubic-bezier(), steps()
a comma starts another property's transition

blocks.text: Animate `transform` and `opacity` when you can. Changing them does not change any box's size or position in layout, so the browser can animate them on the compositor (often the GPU) at full frame rate. Animating `width`, `height`, `top` or `margin` re-runs layout on every frame, which stutters on busy pages.
People who get dizzy from motion switch on **Reduce motion** in macOS. Respect it with `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`: remove movement and pulsing.

--- css .badge { position: relative; display: inline-block; padding: 4px 12px; border-radius: 999px; font-weight: 600; color: white; background: #1a7f37; transition: background-color 300ms ease, transform 150ms ease-out; } .badge:hover { transform: scale(1.08); } .badge[data-state="degraded"] { background: #9a6700; } .badge[data-state="down"] { background: #b00020; } .badge[data-state="down"]::after { content: ""; position: absolute; inset: 0; border-radius: inherit; border: 2px solid #b00020; animation: pulse 1.2s ease-out infinite; } @keyframes pulse { from { transform: scale(1); opacity: 0.8; } to { transform: scale(1.6); opacity: 0; } } @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .badge, .badge:hover { transition: none; transform: none; } .badge[data-state="down"]::after { animation: none; opacity: 1; inset: -4px; } } --- js const states = ['up', 'degraded', 'down']; const badge = document.querySelector('.badge'); document.querySelector('#cycle').addEventListener('click', () => { badge.dataset.state = states[(states.indexOf(badge.dataset.state) + 1) % states.length]; console.log('nas is', badge.dataset.state); });

blocks.name: transition
blocks.sum: Animate a property smoothly whenever its computed value changes.

how.text: When a style change alters the computed value of a listed property, the browser interpolates from the old value to the new one over the duration, using the timing function to shape progress. Only properties with an interpolable type animate (colours, lengths, numbers, transforms); `display` switches at once unless you opt into discrete transitions, and `visibility` does not fade: it is `visible` for the whole transition whenever either end is `visible`.

A transition needs a *change*: setting a transition and the new value in the same style recalculation (for example on an element you just inserted) jumps straight to the end, because the browser never saw a "before" value.

how.code:
.btn { transition: background-color 200ms ease, transform 120ms ease-out; }
.btn:active { transform: scale(0.97); }

examples.desc: Inspect the transition settings an element ended up with
Log each transition as it finishes on the selected element

gotchas: `transition: all` animates properties you did not intend (including layout ones) and makes changes feel sluggish. List the properties.

blocks.name: @keyframes
blocks.sum: Define a named animation sequence and run it with the animation property.
blocks.syntax: @keyframes NAME { from { ... } 50% { ... } to { ... } }     animation: NAME DURATION [TIMING] [DELAY] [COUNT] [DIRECTION] [FILL];

how.text: Keyframe selectors are percentages of the duration (`from` is 0%, `to` is 100%). For each frame the browser interpolates between the surrounding keyframes. `animation-iteration-count: infinite` loops, `alternate` plays back and forth, and `animation-fill-mode: forwards` keeps the last frame's values after the end.
Animations start when the `animation-name` starts to apply, and restart only if the name is removed and reapplied, which is why toggling a class is the usual way to replay one.

how.code:
@keyframes pulse { from { transform: scale(1); opacity: .8; } to { transform: scale(1.6); opacity: 0; } }
.down::after { animation: pulse 1.2s ease-out infinite; }

examples.desc: See which animation is running on an element
Pause every running animation on the page (handy when inspecting one frame)

gotchas: An animation that "does nothing" is often a name mismatch between `@keyframes` and `animation-name`, or a keyframe block made invalid by a typo. Both fail silently.

blocks.text: Why does it look like that? CSS in DevTools

When an element looks wrong, ask the three-stage question: does the rule **match**, does it **win**, and does the property **apply** in this layout? The real Styles pane in Chrome (Elements > Styles) and Safari (Elements > Styles sidebar) answers all three at a glance:

items.text: Rules are listed **winners first**, most specific at the top, each with a link to its file and line. Click the link to jump to the source.
A **crossed-out** declaration matched but lost the cascade to one above it.
A **warning triangle** marks an invalid property name or value: your typo. Hover it for the reason.

A declaration shown with an information icon or greyed out matched and won but **does not apply** (`width` on an inline element, `justify-content` on a non-flex box). Chrome explains why in a tooltip.
"Inherited from ..." sections show inherited values; "user agent stylesheet" shows browser defaults.

Tick boxes switch declarations on and off. Click a value to edit it; ↑ and ↓ change numbers by 1 (⇧ for 10, ⌥ for 0.1). `.cls` toggles classes; `:hov` forces `:hover`, `:focus`, `:focus-visible` and `:active` so you can inspect states you cannot hold with the mouse.
The **Computed** tab lists final values; expand one to see every declaration that competed for it and jump to the winner.
Flex and grid containers get a small `flex` or `grid` badge in the Elements tree; clicking it overlays lines, gaps and areas on the page.

blocks.text: Edits there live only in memory and vanish on reload, so copy the fix into your file. Chrome's **Changes** drawer (⇧⌘P, "Show Changes") lists your edits as a diff.

This book's drawer has a smaller Elements pane: the live tree, the box model and the key computed values of the selected element. The Console fills the gap, because the whole CSSOM is scriptable. This snippet lists every rule that matches an element and sets a given property, in source order:

Two rules match; `#toolbar button` (1,0,1) beats `.btn-primary` (0,1,0). The snippet skips rules nested inside `@media` blocks (those are `CSSMediaRule` objects with their own `cssRules`), and it cannot read stylesheets from other origins; the real Styles pane has neither limit. Now fix it live in a practice page:

items.text: In **Elements**, click `button#deploy`. The computed list says `background-color: rgb(222, 226, 229)`.
In **Console**, type `getComputedStyle($0).backgroundColor` to confirm it from script.
Find the competitors: `[...$('#page-css').sheet.cssRules].filter((r) => $0.matches(r.selectorText)).map((r) => r.selectorText)`.

Fix it with a selector that outranks `#toolbar button` without `!important`: `$('#page-css').sheet.insertRule('#toolbar .btn-primary { background-color: rgb(10, 127, 156); color: white; }', 3)`. The specificity is (1,1,0), and the button turns teal while Cancel stays grey.
Press **Reload page**: your fix is gone, exactly as it would be in a real browser. In a real project you would now put the rule in the CSS file.

blocks.name: getComputedStyle()
blocks.sum: Return the final resolved value of every CSS property for an element (or one of its pseudo-elements).

how.text: The browser runs any pending style recalculation and, for layout-dependent properties such as `width`, any pending layout, then returns the *resolved* values: lengths in px, colours as `rgb()`, keywords expanded. Read properties with camelCase (`.backgroundColor`) or with `getPropertyValue('background-color')`, which is also the only way to read custom properties.

Compare it with `element.style`, which holds only the inline `style=""` declarations and is empty for anything that came from a stylesheet. Calling `getComputedStyle` inside a loop that also writes styles forces a layout on each iteration, a performance trap covered in [DevTools](#devtools).

examples.desc: The question you will ask most often
Compare the colour of every badge on the page in one table

gotchas: `el.style.color` is an empty string for colours set in a stylesheet. Use `getComputedStyle` to find out what the user sees.

blocks.text: A small reset

Browsers ship a default stylesheet with uneven margins, content-box sizing and form controls that ignore your fonts. Most projects begin with a short reset that removes the surprises without wiping out useful defaults. Save it as `css/reset.css` and link it before your own stylesheet:

Line by line: border-box everywhere; no default margins; no text inflation on iOS rotation; a full-height body with readable line height; media that never overflows and leaves no inline gap; form controls in the page font; long URLs that wrap; a `hidden` attribute nothing can override by accident; a visible keyboard focus ring; and near-zero motion for people who asked for it. That last `!important` is one of its few defensible uses: it must beat every animation on the page.
Common mistakes

items.text: **A typo in a property or value.** `backgroud`, `colr`, `12 px` (with a space), `#b0020`. Nothing errors; the declaration is dropped. Look for the warning triangle in Styles, or compare what you wrote with `sheet.cssRules[i].cssText`.
**A missing semicolon.** The next declaration becomes part of the previous value and both die.
**`//` comments.** CSS only has `/* */`. A `//` line corrupts the selector or declaration after it.
**Fighting specificity with `!important`.** Find the winning rule first. Usually adding one class or the same ancestor to your selector, or moving the rule later, is enough.
**Wrong axis in flexbox.** `justify-content` follows the main axis, which turns vertical in `flex-direction: column`.
**`z-index` that "does nothing".** The element is `static`, or the competitors live in different stacking contexts.
**`width: 100%` plus padding overflowing.** Content-box sizing; the reset fixes it.
**Stale CSS.** The browser cached the old file. Hard-reload (Chrome ⇧⌘R, Safari ⌥⌘R) or tick **Disable cache** in the Network pane while DevTools is open.

task.text: Colour the badges using **attribute selectors only** (do not add classes or change the HTML). Background colours: `up` is `rgb(26, 127, 55)`, `degraded` is `rgb(154, 103, 0)`, `down` is `rgb(176, 0, 32)`. A badge with no `data-state` keeps `rgb(110, 119, 129)`. Text is white in every case.

hints: The selector for "a badge whose data-state is up" is `.badge[data-state="up"]`.
Each state rule has specificity (0,2,0), which beats the plain `.badge` rule (0,1,0) whatever the order.

why.text: The browser re-matches selectors whenever an attribute changes, so the same CSS keeps working when JavaScript later sets `badge.dataset.state = 'down'`. Data attributes carry state; classes describe kinds of things. Keeping them apart makes both the CSS and the JavaScript simpler.

blocks.title: Win the specificity fight without !important

task.text: A theme stylesheet you are not allowed to edit makes every toolbar button grey with `#toolbar button`. Make **only** the Deploy button's background `rgb(10, 127, 156)`. Rules: write your CSS into `#mine`, no `!important`, no inline `style` attributes, and the Cancel button must stay grey.

hints: Compute both specificities: `#toolbar button` is (1,0,1). What is `.btn-primary`?
You need an ID in your selector too, plus at least one class or one more type selector. Use the toolbar's ID, not a new one on the button.

why.text: `#toolbar .btn-primary` is (1,1,0) and beats (1,0,1) in the second column, even though both have one ID. `#toolbar button.btn-primary` (1,1,1) also works. Doubling a class (`.btn-primary.btn-primary`, (0,2,0)) does not, because no number of classes outweighs one ID. In your own code, prefer avoiding ID selectors in CSS altogether so these fights never start.

task.text: The page already reads four tokens: `--bg`, `--fg`, `--card` and `--line`. `:root[data-theme="dark"] { --bg: #0f171c; ... }` has higher specificity than `:root` and so wins wherever both match.

Add `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { ... } }` with the dark values and the page also follows the macOS appearance setting while still honouring an explicit choice.

task.text: On your Mac, create `~/lab/web/css-demo/` with an `index.html` that links `style.css`, and a `style.css` that colours the `h1`. Serve the folder with Python, open it in Chrome with DevTools on the Network pane, and reload twice. Then edit the CSS and reload again. Note the status of `style.css` each time (200, 304, or served from cache), and use `curl` to confirm the server sends `Content-Type: text/css`.

hints: `python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1` serves the current folder. Run it in its own Terminal tab.
`open -a "Google Chrome" http://127.0.0.1:8000/` opens the page. Untick and tick **Disable cache** in the Network pane to compare.

After you edit the file its modification time changes and the next request is a `200` again. With **Disable cache** ticked every request is a fresh `200`, which is what you want while developing.

questions.q: Which selector wins for `color` on a link inside `<nav id="nav">`: `#nav a` or `nav a.active.current`?

options.text: `nav a.active.current`, because it has more parts
`nav a.active.current`, because it comes later in the file

questions.why: Specificity compares the ID column first. One ID beats any number of classes, and order only matters when the triples are equal.

questions.q: `.box { width: 200px; padding: 20px; border: 5px solid; }` with the default `box-sizing`. How wide is the border box?
questions.why: With `content-box`, width is the content only: 200 + 2 × 20 + 2 × 5 = 250. With `border-box` it would be 200.

questions.q: You write `.card { colour: red; padding: 8px; }`. What does the browser do?

options.text: Prints an error in the Console

questions.why: CSS error recovery drops only the declaration it does not understand. That is why typos are silent; DevTools marks the dropped line with a warning icon.

questions.q: Which of these properties is inherited by default?
questions.why: Text properties such as `color`, `font-*` and `line-height` inherit; box properties such as margin, border, padding and background do not.

questions.q: A modal with `position: fixed; z-index: 9999` appears behind a header with `z-index: 10`. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: An ancestor of the modal creates a stacking context (for example with `transform` or `opacity`), so 9999 only counts inside it
The header comes later in the HTML

questions.why: `z-index` only competes within a stacking context. The ancestor's context is painted as one unit at its own level, below the header.

questions.q: Which property and value make `width` include padding and border?
questions.why: `box-sizing: border-box` makes the declared width the border box. Apply it to `*, *::before, *::after` in your reset.

blocks.text: Glossary and next steps

Next: [JavaScript Fundamentals](#js-basics) gives you the language that has been changing `dataset`, classes and custom properties in these playgrounds, from values and types to arrays, objects and JSON.

terms.def: The algorithm that picks one winning declaration per property per element: origin and importance, inline styles, layers, specificity, then order
The (IDs, classes, types) weight of a selector, compared column by column to break ties in the cascade
The pattern before a declaration block that decides which elements a rule applies to
One property: value pair inside a rule
A selector part with one colon that matches by state or position, such as :hover or :nth-child()
A selector part with two colons that styles part of an element or generates a box, such as ::before
The CSS Object Model: parsed stylesheets as objects that JavaScript reads through document.styleSheets
A property's value after the cascade and inheritance, with relative units resolved, as getComputedStyle reports it
Content, padding, border and margin: the four layers that make up every element's box
Adjacent vertical margins in block flow merging into the larger one
A direct child of a display: flex container, sized by flex-basis, flex-grow and flex-shrink
One column or row of a grid, sized with px, %, fr, minmax() or auto
A group of boxes painted together as one layer, inside which z-index values compete
A condition such as (width >= 600px) or (prefers-color-scheme: dark) that switches a block of rules on or off
A --name property that inherits and is substituted into other declarations with var()
